“From a business perspective, it’s business as usual.”

Colette Kress, $NVDA earnings call

KEY TAKEAWAYS FROM THE CALL

◆ FY28 growth outlook raised. Nvidia now expects 75% revenue growth, up from 70%, on a higher FY27 base. Demand still exceeds supply, but additional capacity supports the increased outlook.

◆ Vera Rubin’s record ramp. Nearly $20B in revenue during its first quarter of production shipments. Major hyperscalers are bringing systems into production in roughly half the time taken with Grace Blackwell.

◆ AI demand is broadening. Agentic AI is driving strong CPU demand. Nvidia expects Vera CPU revenue to more than double in FY28, alongside continued growth in enterprise and sovereign AI.

◆ Financial commitments are growing. Supply commitments reached $390B and guarantees $118B. Management emphasised greater selectivity in customer financing and future commitments.

◆ Leadership transition. The board confirmed a permanent CEO search covering internal and external candidates, ruled out reinstating Huang and established a National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee.

WHAT ANALYSTS ASKED

Joseph Moore, Morgan Stanley

Q: What supports the higher FY28 growth outlook, and does demand still exceed available supply?

A: Both demand and achievable supply have improved. Management remains confident in 75% growth despite the new export controls.

Vivek Arya, Bank of America

Q: Can Nvidia protect its competitive position and retain talent without Huang?

A: Kress highlighted employee commitment, strong technical leadership and customer and supplier support. The board will conduct a thorough CEO search without rushing the appointment.

Timothy Arcuri, UBS

Q: Can Nvidia protect pricing power and margins as customers develop custom AI chips?

A: Management reiterated its 72–73% FY28 gross-margin outlook, supported by pricing adjustments. It gave no longer-term margin target.

C.J. Muse, Cantor Fitzgerald

Q: Will Nvidia become more selective about financing neocloud customers?

A: Yes, future support will be assessed carefully, particularly financing for land, power and data-centre infrastructure. External financing partners will play an important role.

Stacy Rasgon, Bernstein

Q: Are the new financing conditions in neocloud agreements a change in policy?

A: No. Kress said the disclosure clarifies existing arrangements. Commitments depend on customers securing financing and getting infrastructure operational.

Ben Reitzes, Melius Research

Q: Could changing government policies cause an AI investment slowdown in 2028?

A: Management continues to see strong demand and remains engaged with government, but offered no specific assurances about future policy.

Joshua Buchalter, TD Cowen

Q: How does Nvidia allocate scarce supply among hyperscalers, AI labs and neoclouds?

A: Priority depends on data-centre readiness, available financing and credible customer demand. Management said pricing is consistent across customers.

Jim Schneider, Goldman Sachs

Q: How will Nvidia balance buybacks, supplier investment and customer financing?

A: Buybacks remain a priority, alongside financing additional supplier capacity. Customer guarantees will remain selective.

REMAINING QUESTION

◆ Can customer financing and data-centre construction keep pace with Nvidia’s expanded supply commitments and ambitious FY28 growth outlook?

America’s technology infrastructure has apparently decided to take a collective shit, and the people running the federal government are responding with the intellectual urgency of a Comcast customer service chatbot.

Microsoft went down Thursday. The FAA grounded flights nationwide Friday. Monday brought banking failures and a United Airlines ground stop. Tuesday, Apple suffered outages, Marriott experienced problems, and the National Security Agency’s classified internal communications network malfunctioned.

We’ve also seen reported disruptions involving Salesforce, Amazon Web Services, Workday and Anthropic, although those incidents need further confirmation before being lumped into the same timeline. Outlook, Teams, Microsoft 365, Copilot, Apple Music, iCloud, the App Store, airline communications, banking transactions, hotel reservations. Americans rely on this technology to work, travel, communicate and access their money.

The agency responsible for some of the most sensitive intelligence operations in the world experienced an interruption to its classified internal network. The NSA says mission-critical functions remained operational and redundant systems were available. That’s reassuring, but it doesn’t make the underlying failure insignificant.

At this point, asking what the hell is going on seems considerably more reasonable than pretending nothing unusual is happening.

Especially when you consider what Donald Trump and Elon Musk spent the past year doing to America’s cybersecurity workforce.
